web.named_query: ("Keith Sonderling" OR "Courtney Walter") AI artificial intelligence superintelligence policy statements

summary.text: On February 27, 2025, Sonderling described AI's potential to improve productivity and working conditions while emphasizing civil-rights protections and retraining for displaced workers. Writing as deputy secretary of labor on November 24, 2025, he encouraged workers to embrace AI for higher-paying jobs, productivity, and greater fulfillment. On March 24, 2026, he said AI was creating jobs, productivity gains, and entrepreneurship, and called for skills that would let all Americans share in that prosperity.

stance_review.reason: The supplied evidence supports a generally favorable assessment of AI's broad economic and workforce effects, alongside statements emphasizing safeguards and adjustment to displacement. Narrow hiring applications, individual harms, leadership ambitions, and program announcements were not treated as general AI judgments. Full source context was supplied only for the November 24, 2025 article; context-based findings retain its attribution to Sonderling as deputy secretary.

statements.text: We have to look at this in various ways. The first and foremost position is that any use of artificial intelligence in the workforce, and something, obviously, I'm very passionate about, complies with longstanding laws or it's civil rights laws, whether it's health and safety laws, to ensure that it's being used properly on the American workforce to actually help make them more productive, help make their jobs better, safer, more secure. And there's a lot of promise with AI on that. But on the flip side, if we don't have those American values built into it, if we don't have those civil rights protections built into artificial intelligence, not only are people potentially going to be discriminate, but the products are not going to be able to do what they are intended to do.

statements.text: Well, it was very much on the employment side in a very specific context. And what I was arguing there is, if we have it right, we can actually have a contemporaneous record of how an employment decision was being made.
